Week 8 Overview

The Purpose of This Week

You have now completed:

  • 7 weeks of structured TOGAF study
  • 6 weekly quizzes (Weeks 2–7) totalling 250+ practice questions
  • 2 full practice exams (Week 7) with structured gap analysis
  • One complete end-to-end scenario (ANDH — Al-Noor Digital Health, Week 7)
  • A thorough consolidation week (Week 6) covering every critical distinction and exam trap

Week 8 has one purpose: turn your existing knowledge into exam-day performance.

This means:

  • No new topics
  • No new concepts
  • Only consolidation, confirmation, and confidence

The biggest risk in Week 8 is trying to learn new material in a panic. Resist that impulse. The candidate who scores 80% is not the one who crammed a new topic on Wednesday — it is the one who consolidated what they already know and walked in calm.

Study Schedule

Day Activity Time Purpose
Monday Practice Exam 3 — 40 questions, 55 min, timed 3 hours Final benchmark; identify last remaining gaps
Tuesday Flashcard Marathon — 60 structured rapid-fire items 2.5 hours Lock in all high-frequency facts
Wednesday Final Topic Review — 6 condensed topic refreshers + Exam Brain Dump Template 2.5 hours Confirm retention; prepare exam-room mental tools
Thursday Light Scan — master tables only; mental preparation; logistics confirmation 1.5 hours Final check; no heavy study
Friday Rest Protocol — 30-minute light review only; normal day 0.5 hours Cognitive recovery; arrive fresh
Exam Day Exam Day Guide — from wake-up to submission — Execute everything you have prepared

Week 8 Target

  • Practice Exam 3: 80%+ (32/40). If you score below 80%, the Day 4 targeted re-read covers what to do.
  • Exam Day: 60%+ (24/40) to pass. Given your preparation, 70–80% is realistic.

What Has Changed Since Week 7

The difference between a Week 7 score and an exam-day score is confidence and consolidation. After Week 7 you know the material — what Week 8 does is:

  1. Confirm that knowledge under time pressure (Exam 3)
  2. Cement the exact facts and sequences into fast-recall memory (Flashcard Marathon)
  3. Prepare you to write key facts from memory at the start of the exam (Brain Dump Template)
  4. Ensure you are cognitively fresh on exam day (Rest Protocol)

Day 1 (Monday): Practice Exam 3

Instructions:

  • Remove all notes and study materials from your workspace
  • Set a timer for 55 minutes
  • Do not check answers until all 40 questions are answered
  • Apply the two-pass strategy from Week 6: answer every question in the first pass (flag unsure ones), then return to flagged questions with remaining time
  • Target: 32/40 (80%)

After completing, use the Answer Key. For every wrong answer: identify the topic (use the topic tags), re-read the relevant section in the relevant week's guide for 5 minutes, write one sentence summarising what you now understand.

Q1. [ADM] The TOGAF ADM is organized around a central hub representing a continuous process that runs throughout all phases. What is this central process, and what does it do?

A) Requirements Management — continuously receives and distributes architecture requirements to and from every ADM phase
B) Architecture Governance — continuously monitors compliance throughout the ADM
C) Risk Management — continuously tracks and mitigates risks across all phases
D) Architecture Vision — continuously communicates the target to stakeholders

Answer: A — Requirements Management is the center of the ADM wheel. It is bidirectional: it feeds requirements into each phase (so phases know what they must satisfy) and receives updated/new requirements from each phase (as discovery happens). Architecture Governance (B) is a structure, not a central ADM process. Risk Management (C) is a Part III technique, not the ADM center. Architecture Vision (D) is a Phase A output.

Q2. [Governance] An organization's Architecture Board has received a formal request from a project team. The request documents a deviation from the Architecture Contract, explains the business reason the deviation was unavoidable, specifies the risk to the architecture, and commits to a remediation plan with a deadline 6 months from now. What type of request is this?

A) Architecture Change Request
B) Statement of Architecture Work
C) Dispensation Request
D) Architecture Compliance Assessment

Answer: C — Dispensation Request: a formal request to the Architecture Board for a time-limited exception to an architecture requirement. Key elements that identify it: documents a deviation from the Architecture Contract, explains why, specifies risk, and commits to a time-bound remediation plan. Architecture Change Request is when the architecture itself needs to change (not the implementation's deviation from it).

Q3. [ADM] Which of the following BEST describes the difference between the Architecture Definition Document (ADD) and the Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS)?

A) The ADD is produced by the Architecture Board; the ARS is produced by the development team
B) The ADD describes what the architecture IS (the design — baseline and target for all four domains); the ARS describes what the architecture must DO (requirements, constraints, NFRs, assumptions that the architecture must satisfy)
C) The ADD is produced in Phase F; the ARS is produced in Phase E
D) They are the same document referred to by different names in different TOGAF versions

Answer: B — ADD = the architecture design (what exists in baseline; what should exist in target — for all four domains). ARS = the requirements the architecture must satisfy (performance, constraints, quality standards, assumptions). ADD is built in Phases B, C, D and finalized in Phase F. ARS is created in Phase A and updated throughout. They are complementary: ARS specifies requirements; ADD shows how the architecture satisfies them.

Q4. [Scenario — Governance] During Phase G, a compliance review of a deployed payment processing system produces the following findings: The system uses all required integration standards. All performance requirements from the ARS are met. The Architecture Contract specified that all transaction logs must be stored in an immutable audit store — instead, logs are stored in a standard mutable database. The implementation team says the immutable store "wasn't available in time." What compliance level applies to this finding, and what is the recommended response?

A) Compliant — the system meets most requirements; the logging issue is minor
B) Non-conformant — the system actively deviates from the Architecture Contract requirement for immutable log storage; recommended response: submit a Dispensation Request to the Architecture Board with a deadline for implementing immutable storage
C) Consistent — the system uses the same concepts as the architecture
D) Conformant — minor deviations are acceptable

Answer: B — Non-conformant: the system actively deviates from a specific Architecture Contract requirement (immutable audit store). "Wasn't available in time" = a schedule constraint, not a technical impossibility — this is a candidate for Dispensation, not acceptance. Conformant requires meeting the architecture in all significant respects; an audit store compliance deviation is significant (regulatory implications). The correct process: Dispensation Request with remediation commitment.

Q5. [ADM] What is the relationship between Gap Analysis and Work Packages across the ADM?

A) Gap Analysis and Work Packages are both produced in Phase F
B) Gap Analysis is performed independently in Phases B, C, and D; in Phase E, the results of all three gap analyses are consolidated, and related gaps are grouped into Work Packages — coherent units of implementation effort
C) Gap Analysis is performed only in Phase E; Work Packages are produced from Phase E's results in Phase F
D) Gap Analysis produces Work Packages directly — they are two names for the same output

Answer: B — Gap Analysis is performed in Phases B, C, and D (one per domain). Phase E consolidates all three analyses. Related gaps (e.g., a business capability gap + the data entity it needs + the application that must implement it + the technology platform it needs) are grouped into Work Packages — coherent, implementable chunks. This cross-domain grouping is Phase E's unique contribution.

Q6. [Scenario — Continuum] A large telecommunications company is designing its enterprise architecture. It finds that the TMF (TeleManagement Forum) has published a well-established reference architecture specifically for telecoms companies — the TOGAF-aligned eTOM (Enhanced Telecom Operations Map). At which level of the Architecture Continuum does eTOM sit, and how should the company use it?

A) Foundation Architecture — use unchanged as-is
B) Common Systems Architecture — use as a common pattern across industries
C) Industry Architecture — use as a starting point; customise toward Organization-Specific Architecture by adding the company's specific structures, technology choices, and constraints
D) Organization-Specific Architecture — it already represents this company's architecture

Answer: C — Industry Architecture: a reference architecture specific to an industry (telecoms) but applicable to many organizations within it. The correct Enterprise Continuum usage: take the Industry Architecture (eTOM) as the starting point and customize it toward Organization-Specific Architecture. Never use Industry Architecture unchanged — every organization has specific constraints, technology choices, and regulatory requirements that differentiate them.

Q7. [Scenario — Domains] An architect is reviewing a legacy retail company's application portfolio. The CRM system has been described as follows: "It manages all customer relationships and is central to our loyalty programme strategy — losing this would directly harm revenue. However, it runs on a 12-year-old platform that the vendor stopped supporting 2 years ago, cannot integrate with modern REST APIs, and has known security vulnerabilities that cannot be patched." What TIME classification and recommended action applies?

A) Tolerate — it still works, so keep it running
B) Eliminate — the security risk makes it too dangerous to keep
C) Invest — it is strategically important, so invest to fix the platform
D) Migrate — high business value but poor technical health; preserve the customer relationship function by re-platforming to modern technology

Answer: D — Migrate: High business value (central to loyalty strategy, direct revenue impact) + Poor technical health (unsupported, cannot integrate, security vulnerabilities). The function is valuable; the technology is not. Re-platform: move the CRM function to a modern, supported platform. Tolerate requires adequate tech health. Eliminate requires low value. Invest requires good tech health.

Q8. [ADM] Phase H "Architecture Change Management" distinguishes three types of architectural change. A company discovers that a key partner's API has changed its authentication scheme from API keys to OAuth 2.0. The organization's integration layer (part of the deployed architecture) must update its calling pattern for this one external API. The change affects one integration point only and requires no architecture redesign. How should Phase H classify and handle this?

A) Re-architecting Change — initiate a new Phase A cycle
B) Incremental Change — loop back to Phase E/F for re-planning
C) Simplification Change — handle within Phase H; no ADM cycle re-entry needed
D) This is not a Phase H concern — it is an IT operations matter

Answer: C — Simplification Change: a minor, localized change that can be absorbed within Phase H without re-entering any other ADM phase. One integration point updating its authentication method does not require architecture redesign or re-planning — it is a routine operational update managed within Phase H. Re-architecting and Incremental changes require more significant architectural impact.

Q9. [Repository] An architect needs to find the approved technology standards for the organization — specifically to check whether a new database product the project team wants to use is approved, and if so, under what conditions. Which layer of the Architecture Repository should she consult?

A) Layer 3 — Architecture Landscape
B) Layer 4 — Standards Information Base
C) Layer 5 — Reference Library
D) Layer 6 — Governance Log

Answer: B — Layer 4, Standards Information Base: contains all approved technology standards classified as Mandatory, Recommended, Emerging, or Retiring. This is exactly where the architect will find whether the database product is approved (Mandatory/Recommended), in pilot evaluation (Emerging), being phased out (Retiring), or not listed at all (requiring Architecture Board evaluation for adoption).

Q10. [Scenario — ADM] A government ministry has run a complete Strategic Architecture ADM cycle, producing an approved Target Architecture and Architecture Roadmap. Now a large programme within the ministry — digital transformation of citizen services — needs its own detailed architecture that conforms to the Strategic Architecture but addresses its specific technical requirements and delivery timeline. A new ADM cycle is started scoped to this programme. What concept describes the architecture being developed?

A) Capability Architecture — focused on one specific capability increment
B) Foundation Architecture — the most generic reusable level
C) Segment Architecture — a detailed architecture for a specific part of the enterprise, operating within Strategic Architecture constraints
D) Transition Architecture — an intermediate state between baseline and target

Answer: C — Segment Architecture: scoped to one part of the enterprise (the citizen services digital transformation programme), more detailed than Strategic Architecture, and conforming to its constraints. Capability Architecture is more granular still — it addresses a specific deliverable increment within the segment, not an entire programme.

Q11. [Scenario — Content Framework] An architect is documenting ANDH's Business Architecture. She creates: (1) a structured list of all organizational units with their roles and responsibilities; (2) a cross-reference table showing which organizational units perform which business functions; (3) a diagram showing the reporting hierarchy and geographic distribution of all 57 facilities. What are the TOGAF artifact TYPE classifications for each of these, in order?

A) Diagram, Matrix, Catalog
B) Catalog, Matrix, Diagram
C) Matrix, Catalog, Diagram
D) All three are Catalogs — they all list information

Answer: B — (1) Structured list of organizational units = Catalog (an inventory of items with their attributes). (2) Cross-reference table of units vs. functions = Matrix (cross-referencing two sets of items). (3) Hierarchy/geographic diagram = Diagram (visual representation). Catalog → Matrix → Diagram is the correct order for the three items described.

Q12. [Governance] An organization has a mature TOGAF practice. It also uses COBIT for IT governance and ITIL for IT service management. A new architect joins and asks: "Are TOGAF, COBIT, and ITIL competing frameworks — should we choose one?" What is the correct answer?

A) Yes — they overlap significantly; organizations should choose the most relevant one and not use the others
B) No — they are complementary frameworks operating at different levels: TOGAF governs architecture design and development; COBIT provides the broader IT governance, controls, and audit framework; ITIL manages IT service operations. All three can be used together.
C) COBIT replaces TOGAF for governance-mature organizations
D) ITIL replaces Phase G and H — organizations with ITIL do not need those phases

Answer: B — TOGAF, COBIT, and ITIL are complementary. TOGAF = architecture method (design and govern what to build). COBIT = IT governance controls and audit. ITIL = IT service management (run what is built). None replaces the others. Organizations with all three have: TOGAF designing the architecture, COBIT ensuring governance accountability and audit trails, ITIL managing the resulting IT services.

Q13. [Scenario — Domains] A data architect discovers that when comparing two databases in the same organization, the "Customer" record for the same individual has: correct name and address in both systems, but wildly different purchase history — System A shows 12 purchases, System B shows 3. Investigation reveals that System B only receives records from one sales channel, while System A receives records from all channels. All data in both systems is accurate for what each system knows. Which data quality dimension is violated, and where does the root cause lie?

A) Accuracy — the data is wrong in System B
B) Uniqueness — the same customer appears in multiple systems
C) Completeness — System B has incomplete purchase history because it only receives data from one channel; the source problem is incomplete data integration
D) Consistency — the same data looks different across two systems

Answer: C — Completeness: System B has incomplete purchase history — required data (all purchases) is missing because only one sales channel's data is fed to it. The data that IS there is accurate, so Accuracy is not violated. The customer is not duplicated (same record, just incomplete), so Uniqueness is not violated. Consistency would be the same data appearing differently — here the data is genuinely different because System B has less data.

Q14. [ADM] Which of the following statements CORRECTLY describes when Architecture Principles are first established and how they are used throughout the ADM?

A) Architecture Principles are established in Phase A and replaced by project-specific requirements in Phase B
B) Architecture Principles are established in the Preliminary Phase; they are confirmed and refined in Phase A; they govern ALL subsequent architecture decisions in every phase of the ADM
C) Architecture Principles are established in Phase B by the Business Architecture team and applied only to business domain decisions
D) Architecture Principles are optional guidelines that teams may choose to follow

Answer: B — Preliminary Phase: establishes Architecture Principles (with all four components: Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications). Phase A: confirms and refines them. All subsequent phases: every architecture decision must align with the principles. They are not optional, not phase-specific, and not replaced by requirements. Requirements are project-specific and managed in the ARS; Principles are enterprise-wide governance commitments.

Q15. [Scenario — Domains] An architect is designing the data integration strategy for a retail organization with 8 systems that need to share "Product" data. Currently each system uses its own Product data format, requiring 28 bilateral transformations (8×7/2). The architect proposes a solution that will reduce this to 8 transformations. A separate but related question is: which of the 8 systems is the single authoritative source of new Product records. These are two different architectural decisions. What are the correct names for each solution?

A) Both solved by MDM Registry Style
B) The 28→8 transformation problem is solved by a Canonical Data Model (CDM); the authoritative source question is solved by Master Data Management (MDM)
C) Both solved by an Enterprise Service Bus
D) The CDM solves both — it defines the authoritative format AND the authoritative source

Answer: B — CDM solves format incompatibility: reduces N×(N-1)/2 = 28 bilateral transforms to N = 8 transforms (one per system to/from the CDM). MDM solves authority: determines which system is the single authoritative source for new Product records (the system that Creates in the CRUD matrix). They are complementary, not the same solution.

Q16. [Scenario — Governance] A Phase G review finds that a recently delivered system: uses the correct database technology (Mandatory standard from the Technology Standards Catalog), uses the correct integration protocol (Mandatory HL7 FHIR R4 from the Architecture Contract), and meets all performance requirements in the ARS. However, the Architecture Contract also specified that all access to patient records be logged in a structured JSON format — the delivered system logs in a plain-text format that contains the same information. Is this Non-conformant?

A) Yes — any deviation from the Architecture Contract is Non-conformant
B) No — the logging format is a minor implementation detail; this is Conformant with a documented minor deviation
C) Yes — logging format is a Mandatory standard
D) No — plain-text and JSON contain the same information; there is no architectural issue

Answer: B — Conformant: the system meets the architecture in all significant respects; the logging format (plain-text vs. JSON, same content) is a minor, documented deviation that doesn't affect the architectural intent (which is complete audit logging of patient access). This is a judgment call — if the Architecture Contract specified JSON as a security or interoperability requirement, it would be Non-conformant. As a formatting preference with equivalent content, Conformant is the correct level.

Q17. [ADM] In TOGAF, Phase E (Opportunities and Solutions) is described as the phase that "bridges" architecture design and implementation planning. Which of the following activities is UNIQUE to Phase E and NOT performed in any design phase (B, C, or D)?

A) Updating the Architecture Definition Document
B) Performing Gap Analysis for one architecture domain
C) Conducting a formal stakeholder review
D) Consolidating gap analyses from all three design domains and identifying Work Packages that group related gaps into implementable units

Answer: D — Consolidating gap analyses from B, C, and D into a unified picture, then grouping related cross-domain gaps into Work Packages — this is Phase E's unique activity. All other options (updating ADD, Gap Analysis, stakeholder review) happen in the design phases B, C, D. Phase E does not perform new Gap Analysis — it consolidates what B, C, D already produced.

Q18. [Scenario — Domains] An architect is assessing the integration architecture for a logistics company. The company has 25 enterprise systems. Currently they use a Hub-and-Spoke ESB for internal integration — 25 connections to the hub. They now need to allow 50 external logistics partners to access their shipment tracking and order APIs. The partners need authentication, rate limiting, and versioning. Which additional integration pattern is needed for the external access layer, and why?

A) A second ESB — to handle external traffic separately from internal
B) An API Gateway — designed specifically for managing external consumer access with authentication, rate limiting, versioning, and analytics
C) Event-Driven Pub-Sub — so partners can subscribe to shipment events
D) Point-to-Point — direct connections to each of the 50 partners

Answer: B — API Gateway: the pattern specifically designed for external consumer access to internal services. It provides: authentication (partners must authenticate), rate limiting (prevent API abuse), versioning (partners on different API versions), and analytics (usage monitoring). The internal ESB remains for internal integration; the API Gateway sits at the edge for external partners. P2P with 50 partners = 50 unmanaged connections (unscalable). Pub-Sub would work for event notifications but not for synchronous API queries.

Q19. [Reference Models] The TOGAF TRM taxonomy organizes technology services into categories. An architect is selecting a monitoring and alerting tool for production infrastructure. In which TRM category does this fall?

A) Data Management Services
B) Security Services
C) Network Services
D) Systems Management Services

Answer: D — Systems Management Services: the TRM category covering infrastructure monitoring, alerting, performance management, capacity planning, and operational tools. Data Management Services covers databases and data storage. Security Services covers authentication, authorization, and encryption. Network Services covers networking infrastructure. Monitoring tools — because they manage the operational state of systems — fall under Systems Management.

Q20. [Scenario — ADM] An architect at a financial services firm says: "We have completed our Target Architecture for the entire enterprise. But our mortgage division is in a completely different situation from our retail banking division — they have different systems, different regulatory constraints, and different transformation timelines. We cannot run one ADM cycle that satisfies both." What is the TOGAF-recommended approach?

A) Run two completely separate TOGAF implementations — one for each division
B) Skip architecture for whichever division is more complex
C) Use Architecture Partitioning: the enterprise Strategic Architecture sets the overall direction; separate Segment Architecture cycles are run for the mortgage division and the retail banking division, each conforming to the Strategic Architecture while addressing division-specific requirements
D) Combine both divisions' requirements into one very large Phase B

Answer: C — Architecture Partitioning: dividing the enterprise architecture work into manageable segments that can be developed independently while conforming to the enterprise-wide Strategic Architecture. Each division gets its own Segment Architecture ADM cycle, scoped to its specific needs and constraints, but both must conform to the Strategic Architecture's principles and decisions.

Q21. [Scenario — Governance] An ANDH project is implementing the Patient Portal. The Architecture Contract requires the portal to use TLS 1.3 for all connections. During a Phase G review, the architect finds that the portal uses TLS 1.2 — still a secure protocol but not the version specified. The team explains that their cloud provider's load balancer does not yet support TLS 1.3 but will add support in 3 months. The architecture team agrees this is a temporary constraint, not a team choice. What is the correct process?

A) Accept the deviation informally — TLS 1.2 is close enough
B) Classify as Non-conformant; submit a Dispensation Request to the Architecture Review Committee documenting the TLS 1.2 temporary use, the cloud provider's timeline for TLS 1.3 support, the residual security risk, and a commitment to migrate within 4 months
C) Issue an Architecture Change Request to permanently change the standard to TLS 1.2
D) Reclassify TLS 1.3 from Mandatory to Recommended

Answer: B — Non-conformant (the system deviates from the Architecture Contract). The process: Dispensation Request — formal exception request with a time limit (3–4 months, matching the cloud provider's timeline), documenting the risk and the remediation commitment. D would permanently weaken the security standard across the enterprise, which is inappropriate for what is a temporary vendor constraint.

Q22. [Content Framework] A TOGAF architect asks a junior colleague: "What is the difference between an Architecture Building Block and a Solution Building Block? Give me an example of each." Which response is correct?

A) "An ABB is larger than an SBB — an ABB is a complete system, an SBB is a component within it"
B) "An ABB defines what is needed in conceptual, technology-independent terms (e.g., 'Patient Identity Management Service'); an SBB is the concrete, technology-specific implementation (e.g., 'Oracle Identity Governance Platform v14.3')"
C) "ABBs are produced by project teams; SBBs are produced by the EA team"
D) "They are the same thing — 'Architecture' and 'Solution' are interchangeable prefixes"

Answer: B — ABB = conceptual, technology-independent specification of WHAT is needed (e.g., "Patient Identity Management Service"). SBB = concrete, technology-specific implementation of an ABB (e.g., "Oracle Identity Governance Platform v14.3"). ABBs are defined in Phases B–D (architecture design). SBBs are identified, sourced, or built in Phases E–G (implementation planning and delivery).

Q23. [Scenario — Domains] A retail bank is reviewing its cloud strategy. It has three workloads: (1) Internet banking platform — highly variable demand, 50x spikes on salary payment dates; (2) Core banking ledger — processes all transactions, subject to SAMA regulations requiring data to remain in Saudi Arabia, zero downtime tolerance; (3) Staff HR portal — internal use only, low criticality, low variability. Match each workload to the most appropriate cloud deployment model.

A) All three on Private Cloud for maximum control
B) (1) Public Cloud — elastic scaling for variable demand; (2) Private Cloud in KSA — regulatory data residency + maximum control for critical system; (3) Public Cloud — cost-efficient for low-criticality internal workload
C) All three on Public Cloud for cost efficiency
D) (1) Hybrid Cloud; (2) Multi-Cloud; (3) Private Cloud

Answer: B — (1) Public Cloud: elastic scaling handles 50x demand spikes cost-effectively; not subject to strict data residency (customer-facing but not transaction-level). (2) Private Cloud in KSA: SAMA data residency requires KSA geography; zero downtime = maximum control needed. (3) Public Cloud: HR portal is internal, low criticality, low traffic — public cloud is cost-efficient and fit for purpose. This is requirements-driven technology selection — TOGAF's core principle.

Q24. [ADM] In TOGAF, the Architecture Sponsor and the Architecture Board have distinct roles. Which statement CORRECTLY describes the difference?

A) The Architecture Sponsor chairs the Architecture Board
B) The Architecture Sponsor is the executive who champions and funds a specific architecture initiative and approves the Statement of Architecture Work; the Architecture Board is the governance body that reviews and approves architectures, grants Dispensations, and maintains standards
C) The Architecture Board commissions the architecture; the Architecture Sponsor delivers it
D) They are different names for the same role in different organizational contexts

Answer: B — Architecture Sponsor: the executive champion of a specific project — approves the Statement of Architecture Work (the project mandate). Architecture Board: the governance body — reviews and approves architectures, grants/denies Dispensations, maintains standards, arbitrates architecture disputes. They are distinct roles: the Sponsor funds and mandates; the Board governs and approves.

Q25. [Scenario — Continuum] An architect is looking for reusable architecture assets for a new cloud security architecture. She searches the Architecture Repository and finds: a generic security framework applicable to any technology environment (no organization-specific assumptions), a security reference architecture designed for cloud environments used by multiple organizations in the financial sector, and the organization's own approved security patterns from previous projects. At which Enterprise Continuum levels do each of these sit?

A) All three at Organization-Specific level
B) Generic security framework = Foundation Architecture; financial sector cloud security = Industry Architecture; organization's own patterns = Organization-Specific Architecture
C) Generic = Common Systems; financial sector = Foundation; own patterns = Segment
D) All three at Foundation Architecture level

Answer: B — Foundation Architecture = the most generic, applicable to any organization in any industry (generic security framework). Industry Architecture = specific to an industry sector (financial sector cloud security reference architecture). Organization-Specific Architecture = the organization's own patterns from its own projects. This maps directly to the four levels: Foundation → Common Systems → Industry → Organization-Specific.

Q26. [Scenario — Views] The ANDH CISO has three specific concerns about the new architecture: (1) which data entities contain patient personal information; (2) which systems can read or modify patient personal information; (3) what encryption and access control mechanisms apply to each system containing patient data. An architect creates a single architecture view that addresses all three concerns simultaneously. What would this view contain?

A) An Organizational Map showing data governance roles
B) A combined view using a Data Entity Catalog (showing entities and PII classification) + Data Entity/Application Matrix (showing which systems access which entities) + Data Security Diagram (showing encryption and access controls per system)
C) A Business Process Diagram showing the patient data lifecycle
D) An Architecture Vision summarising the security posture

Answer: B — The CISO's concerns require: (1) which entities are PII → Data Entity Catalog with PII classification; (2) which systems access them → Data Entity/Application Matrix (CRUD); (3) what controls apply → Data Security Diagram. A single "Data Security View" that combines these three artifact types satisfies all three concerns. This is the Concern → Viewpoint → View chain applied: CISO's three concerns → a Security Viewpoint → a composite View.

Q27. [ADM] TOGAF describes the relationship between Architecture Principles established in the Preliminary Phase and the work done in Phase A. Which statement MOST accurately describes this relationship?

A) Phase A creates Architecture Principles for the first time
B) Phase A ignores Architecture Principles — they are only relevant to Phases B, C, D
C) Phase A confirms, refines, and communicates the Architecture Principles established in the Preliminary Phase to stakeholders; it does not create new principles but validates that the existing principles are appropriate for the specific architecture initiative
D) Phase A replaces Architecture Principles with project-specific requirements

Answer: C — Phase A confirms and refines Preliminary Phase principles — it validates that the existing enterprise-wide principles apply to this specific initiative, communicates them to stakeholders, and may refine their expression for this context. Phase A does not create new principles from scratch (that is Preliminary Phase work) and does not replace principles with requirements (requirements are captured in the ARS alongside the principles).

Q28. [Scenario — Frameworks] A large government agency uses TOGAF for its enterprise architecture programme. An audit committee asks: "How do we know that the architecture decisions being made are accountable, auditable, and consistent with enterprise risk policy?" The agency's chief architect says: "Our TOGAF Architecture Governance framework addresses this — we have an Architecture Board with formal decision rights, Architecture Decision Records in the Governance Log, and Compliance Assessments for every project. We also use COBIT alongside TOGAF for the broader governance and audit framework." Is this approach correct?

A) No — TOGAF's governance should be sufficient; adding COBIT creates duplication
B) No — COBIT replaces TOGAF's governance mechanisms
C) Yes — TOGAF Architecture Governance provides architecture-specific governance; COBIT provides the broader IT governance framework, risk management policy, and audit structure. The two are complementary — Architecture Board decisions can be aligned with COBIT governance bodies, and Compliance Assessments can be aligned with COBIT audit processes.
D) Yes — but the agency should choose between COBIT and ITIL, not use both alongside TOGAF

Answer: C — TOGAF + COBIT is the correct complementary combination for this requirement. TOGAF = architecture governance (what to build, architecture decisions, compliance to architecture). COBIT = IT governance (accountability, risk management, audit). They cover different governance dimensions. For government agencies with audit accountability requirements, this combination is specifically recommended.

Q29. [Scenario — Domains] An e-commerce company assesses its Order Management System (OMS): it handles all order processing, is core to revenue generation, and drives 40% of total IT spend. The OMS runs on a modern cloud-native platform with the latest vendor support, good integration capabilities, and strong performance. A new microservices-based order platform is available in the market. What TIME classification applies to the OMS, and what is the recommended action?

A) Migrate — move to the new microservices platform
B) Eliminate — the new platform makes the OMS redundant
C) Invest — high business value and good technical health; actively maintain and grow the investment in the current OMS
D) Tolerate — keep running but don't invest further

Answer: C — Invest: high business value (core revenue, 40% of IT spend) + good technical health (modern cloud-native, current support). The recommended action is to actively maintain and invest in the OMS — add features, scale it, improve performance. The existence of a new platform in the market is not a reason to Migrate if the current platform is healthy and strategic. Migrate is for high value + poor tech health.

Q30. [ADM] An organization is developing architecture for a complex financial services transformation. The Architecture Sponsor has approved the Statement of Architecture Work. The architect now begins Phase B. Which document does the architect use as the primary input to understand WHAT the architecture must achieve (requirements, performance targets, constraints)?

A) Architecture Vision — it contains the high-level aspirational direction
B) Architecture Principles — they contain the governance rules
C) Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) — it contains the specific requirements, non-functional requirements, constraints, and assumptions
D) Architecture Roadmap — it contains the planned sequence of work

Answer: C — ARS: the living document containing all requirements, non-functional requirements, constraints, and assumptions that the architecture must satisfy. Phase B reads the ARS to understand what the Business Architecture must achieve. The Architecture Vision provides direction but not specific requirements. The Architecture Roadmap does not exist yet at Phase B. Architecture Principles provide governance rules, not requirements.

Q31. [Scenario — Continuum] An architect explains the TOGAF Solutions Continuum to a new team member: "When you are implementing an architecture, you don't start from scratch. Just as the Architecture Continuum gives you reusable architecture designs, the Solutions Continuum gives you reusable implementations — products, systems, and services at different levels of specificity." The team member asks: "What's at the most generic end of the Solutions Continuum?" What is the correct answer?

B) Industry Solutions — available for any organization in the same industry
C) Foundation Solutions — the most generic implementations applicable to any organization (e.g., standard networking protocols, operating systems, generic platform components)
D) Common Systems Solutions — general-purpose systems used across many organizations

Answer: C — Foundation Solutions: the most generic end of the Solutions Continuum — implementations applicable to virtually any organization regardless of industry (e.g., TCP/IP network protocols, Linux OS, PostgreSQL database). These are the raw "building block" implementations from which more specific solutions are assembled. The most specific end is Organization-Specific Solutions.

B) Phase G — Compliance Assessments, Architecture Board recommendations
C) Phase E — Architecture Roadmap v0.1, Work Packages (cross-domain grouped gaps), Transition Architectures (intermediate operational states)
D) Phase H — Change evaluation, Architecture Debt tracking

Q33. [Governance] An Architecture Board reviews the compliance assessment for a large project and assigns the following compliance levels to different aspects of the delivered solution: the integration layer "Conforms," the data model "Fully Conforms," the security controls "are Consistent with the architecture vocabulary but have no direct relationship to the architecture design," and the technology platform "Conforms." What is the OVERALL compliance rating, and what action is required for the security controls?

B) Overall: the weakest element determines the action: the security controls being Consistent (not Conformant) means they do not implement the architecture design — the team must be engaged to align the security controls with the Architecture Contract

D) Overall: Non-conformant — all elements must be Fully Conformant

Answer: B — The overall compliance is determined by the weakest finding. Key rule: The more specific the starting point you can find, the better. Use the most specific existing asset and customize from there.

TRM: A TAXONOMY of technology service categories. Used in Phase D. Answers: "What types of technology do we need?" Key categories include: Data Management Services, Security Services, Network Services, Systems Management Services, Integration Services.

III-RM: An ARCHITECTURE PATTERN for boundaryless information flow. Shows how Business Applications, Infrastructure Applications, and Application Platform interoperate. Used in Phases C and D.

TRM vs III-RM: TRM = what categories exist (taxonomy). III-RM = how the layers connect (pattern).

Both live in: Layer 5 — Reference Library of the Architecture Repository.

Refresher 5: Content Framework

Three types of architecture artifacts:

Type What it is Examples
Catalog An inventory list with attributes Application Portfolio Catalog, Technology Standards Catalog, Data Entity Catalog
Matrix A cross-reference between two sets Application/Business Function Matrix, Data Entity/Application Matrix (CRUD)
Diagram A visual representation Business Capability Map, Data Flow Diagram, Infrastructure Diagram

Deliverables vs. Artifacts:

  • Deliverable = formally contracted and signed off (e.g., ADD, ARS, Architecture Contract)
  • Artifact = a component within a deliverable (e.g., ERD, Capability Map, CRUD Matrix)

Building Blocks:

  • ABB = Architecture Building Block = conceptual, technology-independent specification of WHAT is needed
  • SBB = Solution Building Block = concrete, technology-specific implementation of an ABB
  • ABBs defined in Phases B–D; SBBs identified/built in Phases E–G

The most important matrices per domain:

Domain Key Matrix What it reveals
Business Business Function/Organization Matrix Duplication; separation-of-duties risks
Data Data Entity/Business Function Matrix (CRUD) Data ownership (who Creates each entity)
Application Application/Business Function Matrix Gaps (no app supports a function) and redundancies
Technology Application/Technology Matrix Which apps run on which tech platforms

Refresher 6: Architecture Domains — Final Applied Facts

Business Architecture Motivation Model:

  • ENDS (most → least abstract): Vision → Goal → Objective (SMART)
  • MEANS (most → least abstract): Mission → Strategy → Tactic
  • Objective is SMART; Goal is qualitative

Value Chain vs. Value Stream:

  • Value Chain (Porter) = generic categories of ALL value-creating activities (strategic, same for all companies in an industry)
  • Value Stream = specific end-to-end delivery sequence for ONE outcome for ONE stakeholder

MDM styles trigger words:

  • "Cannot modify legacy systems; need cross-references" → Registry
  • "Central copy for reporting; systems unchanged" → Consolidation
  • "Both central and operational are authoritative; transition state" → Coexistence
  • "Central is the ONLY authority; maximum quality control" → Centralized

Integration pattern trigger words:

  • "Too many connections; N×(N-1)/2 problem" → ESB/Hub-and-Spoke (reduces to N)
  • "External partners need access; auth, rate limiting, versioning" → API Gateway
  • "Async; source must not wait; one-to-many notification" → Event-Driven/Pub-Sub
  • "Large app; independent teams; independent scaling" → Microservices
  • "2–4 stable, simple systems" → Point-to-Point is acceptable

Framework integration one-liners:

  • TOGAF + ITIL: TOGAF designs; ITIL manages. Phase G ↔ Change Management. Phase H ↔ Problem Management.
  • TOGAF + COBIT: TOGAF = architecture method. COBIT = IT governance controls and audit.
  • TOGAF + PRINCE2/PMBOK: Architecture Contracts → project SOW. Work Packages → projects.
  • TOGAF + Agile/SAFe: Architecture Runway. EA stays ahead of teams. Abbreviated ADM cycles.
  • TOGAF + Zachman: TOGAF = process (develop). Zachman = classification (organize artifacts).
  • TOGAF + DAMA: TOGAF = WHAT (data architecture). DAMA = HOW and WHO (data management).

Day 5 (Friday): Rest Protocol

The Rest Protocol

Day 5 is not a study day. It is a recovery day. Cognitive performance on exam day is directly affected by sleep quality the night before. Everything you do on Friday should support that goal.

Allowed — 30 minutes total:

  • Scan the Brain Dump Template once (confirm you still remember the 5 items)
  • Read through your personal notes on your 2–3 weakest topics — not to learn, just to confirm

Not allowed:

  • Taking any timed practice tests
  • Reading entire week guides
  • Starting new topics
  • Staying up late

What to do instead:

  • Physical activity (walk, gym, anything that gets you out of study mode)
  • Normal social activity
  • Normal meals — avoid heavy food that might disrupt sleep
  • Light entertainment — not exam-related content

The sleep rule: Be in bed at a time that allows 7–8 hours before your exam start time. If your exam is at 10:00, be in bed by 23:00 at the latest.

If anxiety keeps you awake: This is normal and expected. The anxiety is not a sign that you are unprepared — it is a sign that you care. Use this reframe: "I have done 8 weeks of preparation. 250+ practice questions. Three full mock exams. I know this material. The exam is an opportunity to demonstrate what I already know."

Day 6/7: Exam Day Guide

Before the Exam

The night before:

  • Re-read the Brain Dump Template one last time (5 minutes)
  • Lay out everything you need: ID, directions/login details, water
  • Sleep at your planned time

Morning of exam:

  • Wake at your normal time (earlier is fine; do not sleep extra — it disrupts rhythm)
  • Eat a normal, moderate meal — avoid high-sugar foods (energy crash risk) and very heavy meals (cognitive sluggishness)
  • Arrive at the Pearson VUE test center 20 minutes early, OR complete online check-in 15 minutes before
  • Bring: valid passport or government ID

At the Pearson VUE test center:

  • You will be issued scratch paper (or a whiteboard and marker)
  • Before starting the exam, spend the first 2 minutes writing your Brain Dump Template
  • Do this before reading question 1 — while the facts are freshest

During the Exam — The Strategy

Time budget: 40 questions in 60 minutes = 90 seconds per question average.

Two-pass approach:

Pass 1 — 40 minutes: Go through all 40 questions sequentially. For each:

  • If you know the answer confidently → select it; move on
  • If you are unsure → make your best guess, FLAG the question, move on
  • Never spend more than 2 minutes on any single question in Pass 1

After Pass 1: all 40 questions have an answer. You cannot run out of time with blank answers.

Pass 2 — 15 minutes: Return only to flagged questions. With the rest of the exam in context and fresh eyes, some flagged questions become clearer. Revise if you are now more confident. Do not revise confident answers.

Final 5 minutes: Quick check — any blank answers? Any obvious misreads? Submit.

Answering Recall Questions

Read the question. Before looking at the options — what is the answer?

Then scan options. Match your answer to an option. Done.

If you don't know: eliminate what you know is wrong. Two options left = 50/50. Choose and flag.

Watch for: "BEST describes," "PRIMARY purpose," "MOST accurately" — these signal that multiple options are partially right; you need the STRONGEST one. Watch for: "NOT," "EXCEPT," "CANNOT" — these reverse the logic; the wrong answers become correct.

Answering Scenario Questions

Apply the 4-step approach:

  1. Read the scenario — understand the situation before reading the question
  2. Identify the TOGAF context — which phase, domain, concept, artifact, or framework is operating here?
  3. Read the question — what specifically is being asked?
  4. Scan options and eliminate — wrong category first, then wrong phase, then degree of fit

Context recognition triggers (commit these to memory):

Scenario describes... TOGAF concept
Setting up EA practice before any project Preliminary Phase
Getting sponsorship and scoping an architecture project Phase A
Designing what the business must look like Phase B
Defining data entities, quality, MDM Phase C Data Architecture
Rationalising applications, integration design Phase C Application Architecture
Cloud, HA/DR, technology standards Phase D
"What to do and in what sequence" after design Phase E
"Detailed planning and contracts" for implementation Phase F
Checking whether what was built matches what was designed Phase G
Post-deployment monitoring and change management Phase H
A minor change that doesn't affect architecture Simplification Change
A significant change needing re-planning Incremental Change
A fundamental change needing complete redesign Re-architecting Change
"Too many system connections, N×(N-1)/2 problem" ESB/Hub-and-Spoke
"External partners need managed API access" API Gateway
"Async, fire-and-forget, one-to-many notification" Event-Driven / Pub-Sub
"Uses same vocabulary, no direct relationship" Consistent (compliance level)
"Actively conflicts with the architecture" Non-conformant
"Time-limited exception with a remediation plan" Dispensation
"Formal document specifying what to build + how compliance measured" Architecture Contract

Mental Strategies for Hard Questions

When you encounter a question you truly don't know:

  • Don't panic — hard questions appear for every candidate; the exam doesn't require perfection
  • Eliminate what you know is wrong (usually 1–2 options)
  • Between the remaining options, choose the one that is more specific / more formally TOGAF-correct
  • Flag it, mark your best guess, move on

When two options seem equally correct:

  • One is more directly TOGAF-compliant and the other paraphrases the concept loosely — choose the TOGAF-precise one
  • One is about the right topic but the wrong phase — eliminate it
  • One option uses language from TOGAF ("Architecture Contract," "Dispensation," "Compliance Assessment") — favour it over non-TOGAF paraphrases

When a question seems impossible:

  • Re-read the question carefully — look for "NOT," "EXCEPT," "CANNOT"
  • Re-read the scenario — what phase is operating? Which governance action is happening?
  • Trust your preparation — after 8 weeks, your intuition is more reliable than you think

If you feel time pressure:

  • Check your pace: if 30 minutes have passed, you should have 20+ questions answered
  • If behind pace: use 30-second answers for questions you are stuck on — flag them and return
  • The two-pass approach protects you: every question has an answer after Pass 1

After the Exam

If you pass: You will see your score immediately at the Pearson VUE test center (or shortly after online). Print or save the confirmation. Your certificate will arrive from The Open Group within a few days.

If you do not pass: Understand that TOGAF Level 1 has no restriction on retakes — you can attempt again as many times as needed. Review your score report to see which topic areas were weakest. Use the Week 6 Targeted Re-study Guide to focus your next preparation period. Most candidates who do not pass on the first attempt do so on the second, typically within 4–6 weeks.

Either way: You have completed an 8-week intensive certification programme. The knowledge you have built — TOGAF methodology, enterprise architecture principles, governance frameworks, domain architectures — is professionally valuable regardless of the exam outcome on any given day.
